lesson.title: Reading the Energy Ledger: Enthalpy Change in Reactions
lesson.summary: The enthalpy change of a reaction, delta H(rxn), quantifies exactly how much energy is released or absorbed as written in a balanced chemical equation, and it scales directly with the number of moles that react.
lesson.body:
For any chemical reaction, the enthalpy change is defined as delta H(rxn) = H(products) minus H(reactants). A negative value means the products hold less enthalpy than the reactants, so energy was released to the surroundings as the reaction proceeded, an exothermic reaction. A positive value means the products hold more enthalpy than the reactants, so energy had to be absorbed from the surroundings, an endothermic reaction. Combustion reactions are a familiar exothermic example, releasing energy as heat and light, while many dissolution and phase change processes, such as ice melting, are endothermic, drawing energy in from their surroundings.

A critical detail is that the reported delta H(rxn) always corresponds to the reaction exactly as written, meaning the exact number of moles shown by the coefficients in the balanced equation. This is different from specific heat capacity, which is reported per gram. Enthalpy changes for reactions are reported per mole of reaction as written, so if a balanced equation shows 2 moles of a reactant, the stated delta H corresponds to that full 2 moles reacting, not to a single mole.

This proportionality is what makes enthalpy changes so practically useful: once you know delta H for a balanced equation, you can scale it to find the heat released or absorbed for any amount of reactant, simply by proportion. If you double the amount of reactant, you double the heat exchanged; if you use half, you get half. It also means the reverse reaction has the exact same magnitude of delta H but the opposite sign, since flipping which side is called reactants and which is called products flips the sign of H(products) minus H(reactants).

Consider the reaction 2 H2(g) + O2(g) results in 2 H2O(l), with delta H degree = negative 571.6 kJ as written, meaning 571.6 kJ is released when 2 full moles of H2 react with 1 mole of O2 to form 2 moles of liquid water. Suppose you have only 5.00 g of H2 reacting with excess O2. First find moles of H2 using its molar mass, 2.016 g/mol: 5.00 g divided by 2.016 g/mol = 2.4802 mol H2. Since the balanced equation releases 571.6 kJ per 2 moles of H2, the enthalpy change per mole of H2 is negative 571.6 kJ divided by 2 = negative 285.8 kJ per mole of H2. Multiplying by the actual amount reacting gives (2.4802 mol)(285.8 kJ/mol) = 708.8 kJ released. So burning just 5.00 g of hydrogen gas, less than the mass of a few pennies, releases nearly 709 kJ of energy, illustrating just how energy dense this reaction is. This kind of scaling calculation, moles in, proportional heat out, is exactly the tool Hess's law will build on when you learn to combine several reactions' enthalpy changes to find the enthalpy change of a reaction you never actually ran.
